questions.q: According to this lesson, what two things has this course built up in parallel across its first 22 lessons?
options: The discipline to evaluate an AI system before shipping it, and the discipline to watch, document, and respond to it once it's live
How to write marketing copy for an AI product and how to price it
Only how to build a chatbot, with no other skills covered
How to train a large language model from scratch
questions.explain: Chapters 1-2 focused on evaluation before shipping, and Chapters 3-4 focused on monitoring, documentation, and incident response once live — the capstone combines both.

questions.q: What does this lesson say actually matters most when picking a feature for the capstone?
options: It must be a large-scale production system handling real user traffic
It needs real inputs and outputs you can actually run calls against, not a hypothetical — the feature itself can be simple
It must use the most expensive and advanced model available
It has to be something no one has ever built before
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes a genuine, working, real example over scale or complexity — a simple script calling an API is enough.

questions.q: What are the four deliverables this lesson lists for the capstone?
options: A marketing plan, a pricing sheet, a logo, and a privacy policy
An eval dataset, a monitoring setup, an incident response plan, and a model card
A video demo, a slide deck, a resume, and a cover letter
A GitHub repository, a README, a license file, and a changelog
questions.explain: The four deliverables map directly to earlier chapters: eval dataset (Ch.2), monitoring (Ch.3), incident response plan and model card (Ch.4).

questions.q: Why does this lesson say the capstone 'isn't new material, it's assembly'?
options: Because each deliverable pulls directly from a specific lesson earlier in the course, rather than introducing unrelated new content
Because students are expected to copy another student's completed capstone
Because the capstone requires no actual work from the student
Because assembly means the deliverables are provided pre-made
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly maps each deliverable back to specific earlier lessons (7, 8, 13, 14, 21, 22), framing the capstone as applying prior material rather than learning something new.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the most common way a capstone project goes wrong?
options: Choosing a feature too ambitious to actually finish, rather than doing the chosen work badly
Using too few words in the model card
Picking a feature that is too small and simple to be worth building at all
Spending too much time on the incident response plan specifically
questions.explain: The lesson warns that overscoping — planning something too large to complete — is more common and more damaging than doing a smaller scope imperfectly.
